column2: What does branching give glycogen as a fuel store?

column2: Why does glycogen phosphorylase use inorganic phosphate rather than water, and why is debranching enzyme needed?
column3: Phosphorolysis releases glucose one-phosphate, conserving energy compared with hydrolysis; phosphorylase stops near branches, so debranching enzyme moves a short chain and hydrolyses the alpha one-to-six glucose.

column2: Why does glucose-six-phosphate-dehydrogenase deficiency cause episodic haemolysis?
column3: Lacking mitochondria, erythrocytes rely on this pathway's NADPH to keep glutathione reduced for peroxide detoxification, so infection, drugs, or oxidant foods cause haemoglobin denaturation and membrane damage.

column2: How does NADPH protect cells from oxidants in erythrocytes yet generate oxidants in phagocytes?
column3: Erythrocytes use it to keep glutathione reduced, whereas phagocyte NADPH oxidase transfers its electrons to oxygen to make superoxide inside the phagosome; oxidase defects cause chronic granulomatous disease.

column2: How does the source of blood glucose change from early to prolonged fasting, and how does brain adapt?
column3: Hepatic glycogenolysis dominates early; as glycogen falls, gluconeogenesis powered by fatty-acid oxidation dominates and kidney contributes more, while brain gradually uses ketone bodies, reducing glucose and amino-acid demand.
